label: Tehillim (Psalms) — Part 7 — Psalm 119
summary_plain: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in all of scripture — 176 verses arranged as an acrostic with each section of eight verses beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew aleph-bet. The entire psalm is a sustained declaration of devotion to the Torah of YHWH. Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart. Oh how I love your Torah — it is my meditation all the day. The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Psalm 119 from DSS witnesses (11QPsa and fragments) and the Orit Ge'ez. Psalm 119 is the most sustained Torah-devotion text in all of scripture. Its acrostic structure — 22 Hebrew letters, eight verses per letter, 176 verses total — is a literary monument. Every verse uses at least one of eight key terms for YHWH's instruction: Torah, edot (testimonies), piqqudim (precepts), chuqqim (statutes), mitzvot (commandments), mishpatim (judgments), davar (word), and imrah (saying). The psalm demolishes any claim that devotion to Torah was experienced as legalistic burden. The psalmist loves the Torah. He meditates on it. He runs in its path. He finds it sweeter than honey. The Qumran community's own sectarian texts (1QS, CD) demonstrate the same Torah devotion — the DSS community structured their entire communal life around Torah observance. The NT framing of Torah as bondage (Galatians 3:23-25, Romans 7:6) directly contradicts the witness of Psalm 119 and the entire DSS corpus.

key_terms.definition: The Psalter is organized into five books, each ending with a closing doxology: Book I (Ps.1-41, closes 41:13), Book II (Ps.42-72, closes 72:18-19), Book III (Ps.73-89, closes 89:52), Book IV (Ps.90-106, closes 106:48), Book V (Ps.107-150, closes 150).

Each of the five books of Tehillim ends with a brief doxology of praise to YHWH: 'Blessed be YHWH, the Creator of Yisra'el, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen.' These serve as editorial markers separating the five books.

73 psalms in the Psalter carry the superscription 'le-David' — attributed to or associated with David. These cluster especially in Books I (most psalms) and II, with a smaller group in Book V. 14 psalms also specify the historical occasion in David's life.

Psalms 50 and 73-83 are attributed to Asaph, a Levitical musician appointed by David. His psalms are concentrated in Book III and are marked by historical reflection, wrestling with injustice, and divine-council imagery.

The most common psalm type in Tehillim: a formal complaint to YHWH expressing distress, appealing to YHWH's character, requesting rescue, and often moving to trust or vow. Examples: Ps.22, 42, 69, 88 (the darkest — no resolution).

Psalms of pure praise calling creation and community to celebrate YHWH's character and deeds. Opens with a call to praise, gives reasons, and closes with renewed praise. Examples: Ps.8, 19, 100, 103, 148-150.

Psalms focused on the anointed king — his installation (Ps.2), his rule (Ps.72), his military victory (Ps.20-21), or his covenant standing (Ps.89, 132). After the exile, royal psalms became eschatological — hope for future covenant fulfillment.

Psalms celebrating YHWH's dwelling on Mount Tzion and the security of the city of YHWH. Examples: Ps.46, 48, 76, 84, 87, 122, 132. Zion theology centers on YHWH's chosen presence as the community's foundation.

The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 at Qumran, containing 41 canonical psalms plus additional compositions not in the Masoretic Psalter; its psalm ordering differs from the MT. Demonstrates a fluid, still-forming Psalter canon at Qumran.

The Qumran Psalms Scroll (11QPsa) arranges the psalms in a different order from the Masoretic Text, especially in Books IV-V. This demonstrates that the Psalter's exact sequence was not yet fixed in the late Second Temple period — different communities may have used different orderings.

faq.question: Why is the Psalter divided into five books?
faq.answer: The five-book structure of Tehillim (Psalms 1-41, 42-72, 73-89, 90-106, 107-150) is an editorial organization that parallels the five books of Torah — sometimes called the Psalter as a 'second Torah.' Each book ends with a closing doxology ('Blessed be YHWH... Amen and Amen'). This structure reflects intentional editorial work to shape the collection as a complete, Torah-parallel covenant text.

faq.question: What is a lament psalm and why are they the most common type?
faq.answer: A lament psalm is a formal complaint to YHWH: the psalmist cries out in distress, describes the problem (enemies, illness, abandonment), appeals to YHWH's character and covenant loyalty, and petitions for rescue. Most include a turn toward trust or a vow of praise. Laments are most common because the covenant community's primary need was for a sanctioned, honest place to bring suffering to YHWH rather than away from YHWH. Lament is itself an act of faith.

faq.question: What are royal psalms and how did their meaning change after the exile?
faq.answer: Royal psalms (Ps.2, 20, 21, 45, 72, 89, 101, 110, 132, 144) focus on the anointed king — his enthronement, military campaigns, covenant standing, and YHWH's promises to David's line. After the Babylonian exile ended the monarchy, these psalms became eschatological — the community's hope for future covenant fulfillment under a coming anointed figure. This eschatological reading made royal psalms the most heavily borrowed category in the NT.

faq.question: What is a Zion psalm and what does Zion theology represent?
faq.answer: Zion psalms (Ps.46, 48, 76, 84, 87, 122, 132) celebrate YHWH's presence on Mount Tzion — the city YHWH chose as the divine dwelling place. Zion theology holds that YHWH's presence is the city's real protection: not its walls or armies but YHWH's indwelling. These psalms were the community's liturgical affirmation that YHWH had chosen a specific place to be near the covenant people, making that place sacred by presence rather than by geography.

faq.question: What makes the Asaph psalms distinctive in the Psalter?
faq.answer: The 12 Asaph psalms (Ps.50, 73-83) are marked by: historical recital as teaching (Ps.78), wrestling with the problem of evil and divine silence (Ps.73), divine council imagery where YHWH judges among the elohim (Ps.82), and communal lament over national catastrophe (Ps.74, 79, 80). Asaph is called a 'seer' in 2 Chronicles — his psalms carry a prophetic, visionary quality alongside the liturgical.

faq.question: What does the 11QPsa Qumran Psalms Scroll tell us about the Psalter's formation?
faq.answer: The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 at Qumran contains 41 canonical psalms in a different order from the Masoretic Text, plus compositions not in the MT (Psalm 151, the Plea for Deliverance, the Apostrophe to Zion, David's Compositions list). This demonstrates that in the late Second Temple period, the Psalter's sequence was not yet fixed — different communities had different collections. The MT's 150-psalm order was one arrangement among several.

faq.question: What is the difference between a hymn and a lament psalm?
faq.answer: A hymn (Hallel) psalm opens with a call to praise and focuses on YHWH's character and deeds as the reason for praise — it is praise for its own sake. A lament psalm opens with a cry of distress and focuses on a specific problem requiring YHWH's intervention — it moves from complaint toward trust. Many psalms contain elements of both; Ps.22, for example, begins as an intense lament and ends as a hymn of universal praise.

faq.question: Why do 14 Davidic psalms include specific historical occasions in their superscriptions?
faq.answer: 14 Davidic psalms carry superscriptions linking them to specific events in David's life (e.g., Ps.51 — 'when Natan came to him after he had gone to Batsheva'; Ps.3 — 'when he fled from Avshalom'). These historical notes serve as interpretive keys — they show how individual crisis became covenant liturgy. David's personal suffering was turned into prayer forms that the entire community could use in their own crises, with the historical anchor showing that prayer comes from real life.

faq.question: How does Psalm 100 function as a summary psalm?
faq.answer: Psalm 100 ('A Psalm for Giving Thanks') is one of the Psalter's most compact and complete summaries: a call to universal joyful worship, the reason (YHWH made us and we are his people), the method (enter with thanksgiving and praise), and the theological foundation (YHWH is good; steadfast love and faithfulness endure forever). It crystallizes the Psalter's core theology — creation, covenant, and worship — into five verses.

faq.question: What is the significance of Psalm 145 as the last Davidic psalm?
faq.answer: Psalm 145 is the last psalm with a David superscription and the only one explicitly called 'a song of praise (tehillah)' — giving the entire collection its name (Tehillim). It is also an aleph-bet acrostic, covering YHWH's greatness from every angle. It closes the Davidic collection by affirming YHWH's goodness to all, universal kingdom, and care for the fallen and hungry — before the final five Hallelu-Yah psalms carry the whole Psalter to its doxological end.
